## Observations

1. Square 1 is reachable at the start. Every later square is reachable exactly when it is good and at least one reachable square lies between \(A\) and \(B\) positions behind it.
2. After processing square \(x\), the reachability of the last \(B\) squares contains all the information needed to process square \(x+1\).
3. The same Boolean transition applies at every good square, so powers of that transition can process a whole good run without visiting each square.
4. A bad square shifts the reachability window and inserts a false entry. A run of at least \(B\) bad squares clears the window.
5. The bad intervals are given in order, so they define at most \(M+1\) good runs after square 1.

## Solution sketch

> Square 1 is reachable at the start. Every later square is reachable exactly when it is good and at least one reachable square lies between \(A\) and \(B\) positions behind it.

1. Start with a window of \(B\) bits. Set bit 0 to indicate that square 1 is reachable, and leave all other bits unset to represent positions before the board.

> After processing square \(x\), the reachability of the last \(B\) squares contains all the information needed to process square \(x+1\).

2. Let bit \(j\) represent square \(x-j\). For a good square, the new bit 0 is set if any old bit from \(A-1\) through \(B-1\) is set. For each \(j\) from 1 to \(B-1\), the new bit \(j\) copies old bit \(j-1\). Represent this transition with one input mask per output bit. An output bit is set when its mask intersects the current window.

> The same Boolean transition applies at every good square, so powers of that transition can process a whole good run without visiting each square.

3. Precompute the transitions for \(1,2,4,\ldots\) consecutive good squares, up to the largest power of two at most \(N-1\). To double a transition, replace each output mask with the union of the masks for the intermediate bits it selects. For a good run of length \(g\), apply the precomputed transitions corresponding to the set bits of \(g\).

> A bad square shifts the reachability window and inserts a false entry. A run of at least \(B\) bad squares clears the window.

4. Process a bad run of length \(d<B\) by shifting the window left by \(d\) bits and keeping only its lowest \(B\) bits. For \(d\ge B\), clear the window. If the window becomes empty, print `No` immediately because every subsequent transition leaves it empty.

> The bad intervals are given in order, so they define at most \(M+1\) good runs after square 1.

5. Starting just after square 1, process the good gap before each interval and then the inclusive bad interval. Skip empty gaps between adjacent intervals. After the last interval, process the remaining good squares through \(N\). If there are no bad intervals, this is a single good run of length \(N-1\). Print `Yes` exactly when bit 0 is set after processing \(N\). Each operation preserves the reachability window from the square-by-square recurrence, so this bit gives the required answer. The algorithm takes \(O(B^2\log N+(M+1)B\log N)\) time and \(O(B\log N)\) auxiliary space in integer masks, with each mask holding at most \(B\le 20\) bits. The intervals can be processed as they are read.

usage.note: Codex token counts include its harness context; not comparable to API usage.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
